Add a select:user-invalid rule with border-color #b00020 and a 2px solid border.
Add a select:focus-visible rule with outline 3px solid #1a5fb4 and outline-offset 2px.
Confirm the 44px minimum height is written in the file.

K-017918.example: select { font-size: 1rem; min-height: 44px; } select:user-invalid { border: 2px solid #b00020; } The grep output shows the line number of the min-height rule.
K-017918.check: grep prints a line like 2: min-height: 44px; and the file contains a :user-invalid rule and a :focus-visible rule.
traps: Use :user-invalid instead of :invalid so the error does not show before the user touches the field.
Do not remove the focus outline without a replacement; the focus ring must stay visible.
A 44px height is the minimum touch target, so do not reduce it to 32px for looks.

steps.do: Add an empty span with id='plan-error' and class='error' directly after the select.
Set aria-describedby='plan-error' on the select.
Set aria-invalid to 'true' on the select when its value is empty and remove the attribute when valid.
Count select elements that have aria-describedby to confirm the link is present.
Run an accessibility scan against the page served on port 8000.

K-017919.example: with select aria-describedby='plan-error' links the message to the field. The grep count returns 1 for one select.
K-017919.check: grep -c prints 1 or more, and npx axe reports 0 violations for the select label and aria attributes.
traps: A span with an id but no aria-describedby on the select is ignored by screen readers.
Do not put aria-invalid on the label or the span; it belongs on the select.
Keep the error span in the DOM even when empty, so the link does not break.

steps.do: Start a static server for the site folder on port 8000.
Create the tests folder for the spec file.
Write a test that submits with the placeholder still selected and expects the text 'Please choose a plan.' to be visible.
Write a second test that selects the option with value='basic' and expects the form to submit within 200ms.
Run the Playwright spec file.

K-017920.example: await page.selectOption('#plan', 'basic'); then click submit and expect the success message. The test passes when the output shows 2 passed.
K-017920.check: npx playwright test prints '2 passed' and no failed tests.
traps: Playwright selectOption with an empty string may not match the disabled placeholder, so pick a real value in the valid test.
The static server must keep running in another terminal while the test runs.
Do not assert on a color only; assert on the visible message text.

steps.do: Create the site folders for the HTML, CSS, and JS files.
In site/index.html, add a label with for='plan' and a select with id='plan' and name='plan'.
Make the first option a disabled, selected placeholder with value='' and text 'Choose a plan'.
Add the required attribute to the select element.
Count how many lines in the file contain required to confirm the attribute exists.
Run the axe accessibility runner on the served page and read the violation count.

K-017921.example: <select id='plan' name='plan' required><option value='' disabled selected>Choose a plan</option><option value='basic'>Basic</option></select> The grep count returns 1 when the select has one required attribute. The axe run reports 0 violations when the label and select are linked correctly.
K-017921.check: grep -c prints 1 or more, the select shows a placeholder option with value='' that is disabled and selected, and axe reports 0 violations.
traps: A placeholder option without disabled lets the user submit an empty value, so required never fails. A placeholder with value other than empty string also passes required.
Do not write the error message only in a red color; add real text.
Do not use 'required' on a hidden select without a visible replacement; the browser cannot focus it.

steps.do: Add the novalidate attribute to the form element.
Add a div with id='error-summary', role='alert', and tabindex='-1' above the first field.
On failed submit, fill the summary with one list item per invalid select and call focus on the summary.
Check the form element has novalidate set.
Confirm the page is served with HTTP 200 on port 8000.
Run the axe accessibility runner on the served page and read the violation count.

K-017922.example: A form with novalidate and a div with id='error-summary', role='alert', tabindex='-1' lets your script control the message. The curl command prints 200 when the page loads. The axe run reports 0 violations when the summary is announced correctly.
K-017922.check: grep prints the line with novalidate, curl prints 200, and axe reports 0 violations.
traps: Without novalidate, the browser shows its own bubbles and your summary is redundant.
Do not forget tabindex='-1' on the summary, or focus() does nothing.
Keep the summary text in the DOM after the first error; do not clear it before the user can read it.

steps.do: List onboarding step files and count them.
Write the rule in the plan: show nothing under 200ms, a spinner from 200ms to 1000ms, and a skeleton over 1000ms.
Find every network call in onboarding so you can estimate each step's load time.
Record in the plan which steps get a skeleton and which get a spinner, using the 1000ms cutoff.

K-017923.example: The profile step calls fetch and the plan estimates 1400ms, so it gets a skeleton. The plan Step 2 estimates 300ms, so it gets a spinner.
K-017923.check: The find command lists each step file, and the plan assigns every listed file to nothing, spinner, or skeleton with a time value.
traps: Small models give every step a skeleton, which adds motion to fast steps. Use the 200ms and 1000ms cutoffs. Each step needs a time estimate written in the plan.

steps.do: Write the targets in the plan: LCP under 2500ms, CLS under 0.1, and skeleton height within 4px of the final content height.
List the onboarding route folder to confirm the page the audit will open.
Plan the audit command that measures the performance category against the target route.
Record in the plan the pass rule: the performance score is at least 90 and each target number is met.

K-017924.example: The plan sets LCP under 2500ms and CLS under 0.1 for /onboarding. The audit passes only if the performance score is at least 90.
K-017924.check: The find command lists the onboarding route, and the plan contains three numeric targets, one score threshold, and one lighthouse command.
traps: Small models write targets with no numbers, such as fast or smooth. Every target needs a unit and a value like 2500ms or 0.1. Plan the route path first so the audit targets a real page.

steps.do: Confirm the UI test file that calls the audit exists.
Run only the audit test on an iPhone simulator.
Check that the run reports the test as passed with zero audit issues.

K-017925.example: AccessibilityAuditTests.testLoginScreenAudit calls XCUIApplication().performAccessibilityAudit() on the login screen after launch. The xcodebuild output must end with '** TEST SUCCEEDED **' and report 0 issues.
K-017925.check: The grep shows one line in AccessibilityAuditTests.swift, and xcodebuild ends with '** TEST SUCCEEDED **' with no audit failures listed.
traps: performAccessibilityAudit needs an iOS 17 or later deployment target, so older targets fail to compile. The audit cannot judge whether a label is meaningful, so a label of 'Button' still passes and n…

steps.do: Confirm the row sets a minimum height of 44 points in the form sources.
Run the tap target UI test that asserts each field frame height is at least 44 points.
Check that the test output lists TapTargetTests as passed.

K-017926.example: TapTargetTests.testEmailFieldHeight reads app.textFields["emailField"].frame.height and asserts it is at least 44. The frame value is in points, not pixels, so a 44 point height on a 3x device is 132 pixels.
K-017926.check: The test log shows "Test Case '-[LoginAppUITests.TapTargetTests testEmailFieldHeight]' passed" and ends with '** TEST SUCCEEDED **'.
traps: Padding added outside a field does not raise the hit region of the control itself, so assert the field's frame rather than the parent stack. Writing 44 as pixels instead of points doubles or halves t…

steps.do: Find any fixed frame heights in the input views that may clip larger text.
Confirm the scaled height property uses ScaledMetric.
Run the Dynamic Type UI test that launches the app at the accessibility extra extra extra large size.

K-017927.example: DynamicTypeTests sets app.launchArguments += ["-UIPreferredContentSizeCategoryName", "UICTContentSizeCategoryAccessibilityExtraExtraExtraLarge"] and asserts the email field exists and its frame height is at least 44 points. The field height comes from @ScaledMetric var fieldHeight: CGFloat = 44.
K-017927.check: The test passes, and the frame height reported in the log is at least 44 points at the largest category.
traps: A fixed .frame(height: 44) clips text at large sizes, so use @ScaledMetric for any height that holds text. Testing only the default size misses clipping that appears at accessibility sizes.

steps.do: Confirm the contrast test file states the 4.5 to 1 text threshold and 3 to 1 border threshold.
Run only the contrast tests in the Swift package.
Check that each contrast test case prints passed.

K-017928.example: ContrastTests.testFieldBorderRatio computes the ratio of #767676 on #FFFFFF, which is about 4.54:1, and asserts it is at least 3.0 for a non-text border. The placeholder color #AAAAAA on white is about 2.3:1, so the test must fail for placeholder text.
K-017928.check: swift test ends with "Executed N tests, with 0 failures" and the filtered run lists testFieldBorderRatio as passed.
traps: Placeholder text needs 4.5:1, and many light grey placeholders fail it. Non-text field borders need 3:1 under WCAG 1.4.11, not 4.5:1, so testing one ratio for everything gives wrong results.

steps.do: Confirm the code posts an accessibility announcement for validation errors.
Confirm the error text view has a stable accessibility identifier.
Run the validation UI test that enters an invalid email and checks the error and announcement.

K-017929.example: Entering 'user@' into the email field sets an error state, and the view posts AccessibilityNotification.Announcement("Enter a valid email").post() after the error text appears. ValidationAnnouncementTests asserts app.staticTexts["emailError"].exists is true.
K-017929.check: The grep finds at least 1 announcement call, and xcodebuild ends with '** TEST SUCCEEDED **' with ValidationAnnouncementTests passed.
traps: Posting the announcement before the error view updates means VoiceOver reads nothing useful, so post after the state change. Showing the error only as a red border breaks WCAG 1.4.1 because color alo…

steps.do: Search the source for existing red error classes so you reuse them.
Write in the plan that invalid inputs use aria-[invalid=true]:border-red-600 and the error text uses peer-invalid:block.
Confirm that red-600 text on white meets 4.5:1 contrast; red-600 is #dc2626, about 4.8:1.
Check that the plan uses real Tailwind variants and no made-up class names.

K-017930.example: Input class border-slate-300 is the default, and aria-[invalid=true]:border-red-600 applies when the field is invalid. The error paragraph after the input uses hidden peer-invalid:block so it appears only when the input is invalid.
K-017930.check: The plan lists exactly these two classes, aria-[invalid=true]:border-red-600 and peer-invalid:block, and the contrast figure written is at least 4.5:1.
traps: peer-invalid only works when the input has the class peer and the error element comes after the input in the DOM. A small model often puts the error before the input and the style never applies.
Do not write invalid:border-red-600 for a state that JavaScript sets; the invalid variant follows the native constraint, not your error state.

steps.do: Find any inputs or buttons with a fixed height of h-8 that are too short for touch.
Write in the plan that each input and button uses min-h-11, which is 2.75rem, or 44px at the default root size.
Write in the plan that inputs use text-base, which is 1rem or 16px, so mobile browsers do not zoom on focus.
Count how many form files already use min-h-11 so you know how much to change.

K-017931.example: An input with h-8 px-2 becomes min-h-11 px-3 text-base. The submit button gets min-h-11 too, so both controls are 44px tall.
K-017931.check: rg -c 'min-h-11' src prints a count greater than zero for every form file listed in the plan, and the plan states 2.75rem equals 44px.
traps: min-h-11 is 2.75rem, not 2.75px. A small model may write min-h-[2.75px] or h-11 by mistake, and h-11 fixes the height and can clip wrapped text.
Use text-base for inputs. text-sm is 14px, which can trigger zoom on iOS.

steps.do: Write in the plan that each field validates on blur, and the whole form validates on submit.
Write in the plan that an error must appear within 200ms of blur or submit.
List the existing Playwright spec files so you know where the timing tests will go.
List the Playwright tests that already exist to see what the plan must cover.

K-017932.example: On blur of the email field with the value not-an-email, the error shows within 200ms. On submit with the password empty, every empty required field shows its error at once.
K-017932.check: npx playwright test --list prints a line like Total: 4 tests in 2 files, and the plan has one timing rule per field type with a 200ms limit.
traps: Small models often validate on every keystroke, which shows errors while the user is still typing. The plan should say blur, not change.
Do not write a timing rule without a number; the 200ms limit is what a test can check.

steps.do: Check whether the forms plugin is already in the dependencies.
Find any existing @plugin lines in the project so you add the new one in the same place.
Write in the plan that the plugin is added in the CSS file with @plugin and not in a tailwind.config.js plugins array, because the project uses v4.

K-017933.example: In the main CSS file, below @import "tailwindcss";, add @plugin "@tailwindcss/forms"; so input, select, and textarea get a neutral base style that the error classes can override.
K-017933.check: npm ls @tailwindcss/forms prints a line such as @tailwindcss/forms@0.5.x, and rg -n '@plugin' . shows the new line in the CSS file.
traps: Small models often write the v3 config form, which is wrong for v4 projects. Use @plugin in CSS.
The package name is @tailwindcss/forms. Do not write @tailwind/forms, which does not exist.

steps.do: Find the files that contain a form element.
Count the input elements in the src folder.
Count the label elements in the src folder and check that the total matches the input count.
Write one line per field in the plan with name, type, required yes or no, and max length.
After the form exists, run axe on the signup page and confirm it exits 0 with no label or name violations.

K-017934.example: Field email uses type email, is required, and has max length 254. Field password uses minlength 12 and is required.
K-017934.check: rg -c '<input' src prints a count per file, such as src/SignupForm.tsx:4, the label count for the same file is also 4, and the axe run exits with code 0.
traps: Small models skip the label count, which leaves inputs with no accessible name.
Do not invent rules that are not in the spec. Count only real input elements, not text inside comments.

steps.do: Find any existing aria-describedby attributes so you match their naming.
Write in the plan that each error element gets id name plus -error, such as email-error, and the input points to it with aria-describedby.
Count how many inputs already set aria-describedby, to compare with the field count from the inventory.
Check that the plan keeps ids unique, with one id per field on the page.
Run axe on the form page and confirm it exits 0, which means no duplicate-id or aria-valid-attr-value violations.

K-017935.example: The email input has id="email" and aria-describedby="email-error", and the error paragraph has id="email-error" with the text Enter a valid email. The input also sets aria-invalid when the error is shown.
K-017935.check: rg -c 'aria-describedby' src prints a count equal to the number of inputs in the plan, no id value appears twice in the plan, and the axe run exits with code 0.
traps: Small models often reuse the same id, such as error, for every field, which breaks the link for all but one input.
Do not point aria-describedby at an element that does not exist when the field is valid; keep the error element in the DOM with empty text or hide it.

steps.do: Install the test helpers as dev dependencies.
Confirm the Vitest config uses the jsdom environment.
Run only the EmptyState accessibility spec.
Check the run reports zero axe violations in the output.

K-017936.example: EmptyState.spec.ts mounts EmptyState with title 'No projects yet' and calls axe(wrapper.element). The assertion expect(results.violations).toHaveLength(0) must pass.
K-017936.check: Output shows 'Tests 1 passed' and the axe assertion reports 0 violations.
traps: Mounting without attachTo or passing the wrong element makes the axe check pass vacuously.
Forgetting expect.extend with vitest-axe matchers leaves toHaveNoViolations undefined.
Testing a parent page instead of the component hides the component's own failures.

steps.do: Find the role attribute on the EmptyState root element.
Run the test that queries the live region by role.
Confirm the title sits inside a real heading element.

K-017937.example: The spec calls screen.getByRole('status') from @testing-library/vue and asserts toHaveTextContent('No projects yet').
K-017937.check: Vitest prints '1 passed' for the announces test, and grep shows one line containing role="status".
traps: Using role=alert for routine empty messages is too aggressive, so use status.
Putting v-if on the live region itself means screen readers miss the insertion, so keep the container mounted and change its text.
Forgetting aria-live when the role is not status leaves updates silent.

steps.do: Install Playwright and the axe adapter.
Install the Chromium browser for Playwright.
Start the dev server on port 5173 in a separate terminal.
Run the empty-state accessibility spec.
Confirm the report lists no violations.

K-017938.example: The spec visits /projects with an empty mock API, runs new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(['wcag2aa']).analyze(), and expects violations to equal [].
K-017938.check: Output says '1 passed' and the expect(results.violations).toEqual([]) assertion succeeds.
traps: Scanning before the empty state renders gives a false pass, so wait for the text first.
Limiting withTags to wcag2a skips the AA contrast rules.
Using a route name that differs from the dev server path tests a 404 page instead.

steps.do: List every color declaration in the empty state styles.
Run the axe color-contrast rule against the rendered route.
Confirm body text measures at least 4.5:1 against its background.
Confirm large heading text measures at least 3:1 against its background.

K-017939.example: Body text #6b7280 on #ffffff measures about 4.83:1, which passes. The lighter #9ca3af on #ffffff measures about 2.54:1, which fails.
K-017939.check: axe reports zero color-contrast violations, and the body text ratio is 4.5:1 or higher.
traps: Checking only the heading and skipping the muted paragraph misses the failing text.
Setting opacity on a wrapper lowers the contrast of its children in ways a design token list does not show.
Trusting a color from a design file instead of the computed color in the browser gives wrong ratios.

steps.do: Count heading tags inside the component file, expecting exactly one.
Confirm the section is labelled by its heading id.
Run the heading-order axe rule on the page.
Confirm the heading id comes from useId so instances stay unique.

K-017940.example: EmptyState.vue renders one <h2 :id="headingId"> where const headingId = useId() comes from vue, and the section sets aria-labelledby to that same id.
K-017940.check: grep -Ec prints 1, and axe reports zero heading-order violations.
traps: Hardcoding id='empty-heading' makes two instances on one page clash.
Using an h4 because it looks smaller skips heading levels.
Forgetting aria-labelledby leaves the region with no accessible name.

steps.do: Add a Playwright spec that tabs to the action button and measures it.
Run the keyboard focus and target size spec.
Run the axe scan on the page once more after the change.
Confirm the button bounding box height is at least 44px.

K-017941.example: The spec presses Tab from the page start, expects focus on getByRole('button', { name: 'Create project' }), and asserts (await button.boundingBox()).height >= 44.
K-017941.check: Playwright reports '1 passed', and the height assertion holds at 44 or more.
traps: Testing focus with a mouse click hides missing focus styles, so use the Tab key.
Using a 32px icon-only button and assuming padding fixes it leaves the target too small.
Checking toBeFocused before the button is visible gives a timeout that looks like a focus bug.

steps.do: Confirm the mobile project in playwright.config.ts sets viewport width 375 and height 667.
Write tests/modal-mobile.spec.ts that calls page.setViewportSize, clicks the open button, and reads the panel bounding box.
Assert the panel width is no more than 375 pixels.
Run only this test on the mobile project.
If the panel is wider than 375, change the Modal.vue style to width: 100% with max-width: 90vw.

K-017942.example: The test sets the viewport to 375x667 and reads a panel width of 359px, which passes the 375px limit. Before the fix the panel had a fixed width of 420px and the assertion failed.
K-017942.check: Playwright prints '1 passed' and the process exits with code 0.
traps: Do not assert the panel is exactly 100vw wide, because padding and max-width change that value. Do not read the box before the Transition ends, so wait for the panel with expect(panel).toBeVisible() …

steps.do: Create src/composables/useResponsiveModal.ts exporting useResponsiveModal that returns a ref named isFullscreen.
Write src/composables/useResponsiveModal.spec.ts that stubs window.matchMedia to return matches true for the query '(max-width: 767px)'.
Run the composable spec once with Vitest.
Add a second test that stubs matches false for the same query and asserts isFullscreen.value is false at 768px.
Confirm the composable calls onScopeDispose to remove the matchMedia change listener.

K-017943.example: With the stub set to matches true, isFullscreen.value is true at 767px, and with the stub set to false, it is false at 768px. The test calls the stored change callback to simulate a resize.
K-017943.check: Vitest prints 'Tests 2 passed (2)' and exits with code 0.
traps: Do not read window.innerWidth in the test, because the composable reads matchMedia and the two can disagree. Do not forget to restore the original matchMedia stub in afterEach.

steps.do: Confirm the close button in Modal.vue has a data-testid attribute.
Write tests/modal-touch.spec.ts that opens the modal at 375px width and reads the close button boundingBox.
Assert both box width and box height are at least 44 pixels.
Run the touch test on the mobile project.
If the test fails, set min-width: 44px and min-height: 44px on the close button in the scoped style of Modal.vue.

K-017944.example: The boundingBox for the close button returns width 48 and height 44, so expect(box.height).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(44) passes. The button has min-width and min-height set to 44px in the scoped style.
K-017944.check: The test prints '1 passed' and the measured height is 44 or more.
traps: Do not measure the icon inside the button, because the tap target is the button element itself. Do not stop at 40px, which is below the 44px minimum.

steps.do: Start the Vite dev server on port 5173 in its own terminal.
Open the modal demo route and make sure the modal is open before the scan.
Run axe against the demo URL with a 320px window width and exit nonzero on violations.
Record the number of violations printed by axe.
Fix each violation, such as a color-contrast ratio below 4.5:1 for body text, and run the scan again.

K-017945.example: Axe reports 0 violations at window width 320 after the dialog gets aria-labelledby. Before the fix it reported one color-contrast violation with a ratio of 3.9:1.
K-017945.check: Axe prints 'No violations found' and the process exits with code 0.
traps: Do not scan with the modal closed, because the dialog markup is absent and the result means nothing. Do not treat the 4.5:1 contrast minimum as optional for normal body text.

steps.do: Build the app for production with Vite.
Serve the built dist folder on port 4173 in its own terminal.
Run Lighthouse with the mobile form factor and only the accessibility category, writing JSON output.
Read the accessibility score from the JSON report.
Confirm the printed score is 0.95 or higher before merging.

K-017946.example: The jq command prints 0.97 after the modal received aria-modal and a labelled close button. The same modal scored 0.81 before those attributes were added.
K-017946.check: The jq command prints a number of 0.95 or higher.
traps: Do not use the desktop form factor, because it hides the mobile layout. Do not score the dev server, since its unminified output skews the result; use the built preview instead.

steps.do: Write tests/modal-overflow.spec.ts that sets the viewport to 375 by 667, opens the modal, and reads document.documentElement.scrollWidth.
Assert the scrollWidth equals the viewport width of 375.
List the test names in the overflow spec to confirm it is picked up.
Run the overflow test on the mobile project.
Run the same test on the desktop project at 1280 by 800 to confirm the check still passes.

K-017947.example: With the modal open at 375px, scrollWidth evaluates to 375, so expect(scrollWidth).toBe(375) passes. Before the fix a modal with width 420px made scrollWidth 420 and the test failed.
K-017947.check: Playwright prints '1 passed' for the mobile project and scrollWidth equals 375.
traps: Do not compare innerWidth to itself, because the check needs the page's scrollWidth. Do not run the check with the modal closed, since the overflow comes from the open dialog.

steps.do: Find the tr elements in the table body.
Add transition-colors duration-150 ease-out and hover:bg-slate-50 to each body row className.
Confirm duration-150 appears on the body row className.
Run the TypeScript check to confirm the JSX still compiles.

K-017948.example: A body row className becomes 'border-b transition-colors duration-150 ease-out hover:bg-slate-50'. Hovering the row now fades the background over 150ms instead of changing instantly.
K-017948.check: rg -c prints 1 or more; tsc prints no errors and exits with code 0.
traps: Do not use transition-all on the whole table, since it animates layout and causes jank.
Put the transition on the rows that change, not on the table element.
ease-out is a separate class from duration-150, so both are needed.

steps.do: Find the row className that already has transition-colors.
Add motion-reduce:transition-none to the same className string.
Add motion-reduce:animate-none to any element that uses an animate class.
Write a Playwright test that emulates reduced motion and reads the computed transition duration of a row.
Run the reduced motion test.

K-017949.example: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, a row with motion-reduce:transition-none reports transitionDuration 0s in computed style. Normal users still get 150ms.
K-017949.check: Playwright reports 1 passed, and the computed transitionDuration is 0s under reduced motion emulation.
traps: motion-reduce is a variant prefix, so do not write a media query by hand.
Keep the hover color change; remove only the motion.
Reduced motion still needs visible feedback, such as a color change.

steps.do: Find the sort icon svg inside the sortable th button.
Set aria-sort on the th element to ascending, descending, or none.
Add transition-transform duration-200 and aria-[sort=descending]:rotate-180 to the svg className.
Run eslint on the component to catch invalid class or attribute syntax.

K-017950.example: A th with aria-sort='descending' makes its svg rotate 180 degrees over 200ms. The same aria attribute drives screen reader output and the animation.
K-017950.check: eslint reports 0 errors; after sorting descending, the svg computed transform is close to matrix(-1, 0, 0, -1, 0, 0).
traps: Use the bracket syntax aria-[sort=descending] exactly; a plain sort-descending class does nothing.
Rotate the svg, not the th, so header text stays upright.
Do not rely on color alone to show sort direction.

steps.do: Add a fadeIn keyframe and an animation entry named fade-in under theme.extend in tailwind.config.js.
Add animate-fade-in and motion-reduce:animate-none to each newly inserted tr className.
Build the Tailwind CSS to confirm the animation utility is generated.
Count the generated fadeIn keyframe in the built CSS.

K-017951.example: The config maps animation 'fade-in' to 'fadeIn 200ms ease-out', with keyframes going from opacity 0 to 1. A newly inserted row carries animate-fade-in and fades in once on mount.
K-017951.check: grep -c prints 1 or more, and dist/table.css contains .animate-fade-in and @keyframes fadeIn.
traps: Keyframes belong under theme.extend.keyframes, not as raw CSS in a plugin.
Animate only opacity and transform, since animating height forces layout.
The animation runs once on mount, so re-renders with the same key will not replay it.

steps.do: Find the thead element and its scroll container wrapper.
Add sticky top-0 transition-shadow duration-200 to the thead className.
Set data-scrolled to the string 'true' in a scroll listener when scrollTop is above 0.
Add data-[scrolled=true]:shadow-md to the thead className.
Run the Playwright test that scrolls the table and reads the box-shadow.

K-017952.example: After scrolling 40px, data-scrolled='true' is set and the thead gets shadow-md over 200ms. At scroll 0 the attribute is removed and the shadow fades out.
K-017952.check: Playwright reports 1 passed; computed box-shadow is none at scrollTop 0 and not none at scrollTop 40.
traps: Sticky needs a scroll container with overflow-auto, or it does nothing.
Set the attribute to the string 'true' or 'false' so it matches data-[scrolled=true].
Remove the scroll listener in the useEffect cleanup.

steps.do: Add opacity-0 transition-opacity duration-200 to the row className when its state is removing.
Remove the row from state inside a setTimeout of 200ms that starts when the removing state is set.
